lesson.body:
When grapes ferment, yeast eats their natural sugar and turns it into alcohol. If the yeast eats nearly all of it, the wine tastes "dry" — no real sweetness. If a little sugar remains, that leftover is called residual sugar, and it's what makes a wine taste sweet. Picture a scale: dry, off-dry (just a touch of sweetness, barely there), and sweet (clearly sugary, like dessert). Most everyday red and white wines you'll meet are dry.

Here's the trap that fools almost every beginner: smelling fruit is not the same as tasting sugar. Plenty of dry wines burst with aromas of cherry, peach, or citrus, so your nose shouts "sweet!" before you've even taken a sip. But aroma and sweetness are separate things.

So how do you actually tell? Ignore the nose and pay attention to the taste in your mouth. Take a sip: if it feels sugary, like a splash of soda, it's sweet. If your nose smelled fruit but the taste itself stays clean and not sugary, congratulations — that's a dry wine wearing a fruity costume.
outcomes: Explain how leftover sugar makes a wine sweet
Place a wine on the dry to sweet scale
Judge sweetness by taste, not by fruity smell

deep_notes: Winemakers measure residual sugar in grams per litre. Most dry wines keep only a few grams, too little to notice. There are several ways to stop fermentation with sugar left over: chilling the wine and filtering out the yeast, starting with grapes so sweet that the yeast gives up as the alcohol climbs, or adding grape spirit, as in port, which kills the yeast.

European labels can put this scale into words. For still wines, EU rules use four steps: dry (sec in French, trocken in German), medium dry (demi-sec, halbtrocken), medium sweet (moelleux, lieblich) and sweet (doux, süß). Off-dry roughly matches medium dry. These words are optional, though, so many dry wines say nothing about sweetness on the label at all.

Fruity aromas come from the grape and from fermentation itself, not from sugar. Yeast creates compounds called esters that smell of banana, pear or pineapple. Some grapes, like Muscat and Gewürztraminer, are so aromatic that even a bone-dry version, one with no sugar you can taste, smells lush with flowers, lychee or fresh grapes. Riper grapes from warm places add jammy fruit aromas too, without making the wine sweet.

Sweetness is a taste your tongue picks up directly, so the mouth is the right judge, but it can still be nudged. Alcohol has a slightly sweet taste of its own, so a big, ripe red can seem a touch sweeter than it is. High acidity does the opposite and hides sugar. Cold also mutes sweetness, which is why a sweet wine can seem sweeter as it warms up.

deeper.body: Sparkling wines use their own sweetness words. Brut is dry and is the most common style of Champagne. Brut Nature has no added sugar at all. Confusingly, Extra Dry is slightly sweeter than Brut, and Demi-Sec is clearly sweet. The sugar comes from the dosage, a small dose of sweetened wine added just before the final cork goes in.
deeper.title: The Extra Dry trap

deeper.q: A Champagne labelled Extra Dry is drier than one labelled Brut.
deeper.why: It sounds drier, but Extra Dry is actually a little sweeter than Brut. Brut Nature is the driest of these.

deeper.body: Many of the greatest sweet wines start with super-sweet grapes. In Sauternes and Tokaji, a helpful fungus called noble rot shrivels the grapes and concentrates their sugar. For ice wine, made in places like Germany and Canada, grapes freeze on the vine and are pressed while frozen, so only sweet, syrupy juice runs out. With so much sugar, the yeast stops before it can eat it all.
deeper.title: How sweet wines keep their sugar

deeper.why: Noble rot and freezing both concentrate the sugar in the grape. Early picking and water would do the opposite.

v2.body:
In 2010 divers off Finland's Åland Islands found a sunken ship carrying Champagne, France's famous sparkling wine, about 170 years old. Tests showed well over 100 grams of sugar per litre. Most Champagne today is **Brut**, a dry style with under 12.

Yeast is made of tiny living things too small to see. When grapes ferment, yeast eats their natural sugar and turns it into alcohol. If it eats nearly all of it, the wine is **dry**, which in wine talk means not sweet. Any sugar left over is called **residual sugar** (residual means left over), and it makes a wine taste sweet. It is measured in grams per litre.

Picture a scale. Dry has no real sweetness. **Off-dry** has just a touch, barely there. Sweet is clearly sugary, like dessert. Most everyday red and white wines you will meet are dry.

Yeast will eat every gram of sugar it can, so a sweet wine needs help. Winemakers keep sugar in three main ways:
• Grapes so sweet the yeast gives up as the alcohol climbs, like the shrivelled grapes of Sauternes, a sweet French wine.
• Chilling the wine and filtering out the yeast.
• Adding grape spirit, as in port, a sweet wine from Portugal. The spirit stops the yeast.

European labels may name the sweetness, but it is optional and many dry wines say nothing. For still wines (wines without bubbles), dry (sec in French, trocken in German) means up to 4 grams per litre. It can be up to 9 if the wine is high in **acidity**, the sourness that makes a lemon sharp. Medium dry (demi-sec, halbtrocken) goes up to 12, or 18 with high acidity. Medium sweet (moelleux, lieblich) goes up to 45, and sweet (doux, süß) is 45 or more. Off-dry roughly matches medium dry.

The big beginner trap: a fruity smell is not sugar. Plenty of dry wines smell strongly of cherry, peach or citrus. Those smells come from the grape and from fermentation, not from sugar. Even a **bone dry** wine, with no sugar you can taste, can smell lush: a dry Gewürztraminer or Muscat smells of lychee, roses or fresh grapes. Even the fruit you seem to taste is mostly your nose, smelling from inside your mouth.

So trust your mouth. Take a sip and let it coat your tongue. If it feels sugary, like a splash of soda, it is sweet. If it smelled fruity but tastes clean, it is a dry wine in a fruity costume. Not sure? Pinch your nose as you sip: the fruit fades, but sweetness still shows. Acidity hides sugar. Alcohol tastes slightly sweet. Cold mutes sweetness, so a sweet wine seems sweeter as it warms.
deep_notes: In the 1800s Champagne houses sweetened their wine to suit each market. Champagne for Russia, called goût russe (French for 'Russian taste'), could hold up to about 300 grams of sugar per litre, while English drinkers liked theirs much drier. British taste led the change: the Champagne house Pommery is credited with the first Brut, made for British drinkers from the grapes of 1874. Over the following century, dry Brut became the style most of the world drinks.

The sugars counted are glucose and fructose, the two natural sugars in ripe grapes. Most dry wines keep only a few grams per litre, too little to notice. For comparison, a sugary soft drink holds many times that, which is why the soda test works: when a wine reminds you of a fizzy drink, there is plenty of sugar in it.

Beginners often call a red wine dry when they mean it leaves the mouth feeling dry, like strong black tea. That drying feel is tannin, which comes from grape skins, and it has nothing to do with sugar. A wine can be drying and still carry a little sugar, or be smooth and completely dry, so keep the two ideas apart.

Each word is tied to grams of sugar per litre. For still wines, dry means up to 4, medium dry up to 12, medium sweet up to 45, and sweet 45 or more. Acidity buys extra room, because it hides sweetness: a sharp, fresh German Riesling can be labelled trocken with up to 9 grams, and medium dry stretches to 18. A soft wine with little acidity must stay at 4 or below to be called dry.

Fruity aromas come from the grape and from fermentation itself. Yeast creates compounds called esters, which can smell of banana, pear or pineapple. Riper grapes from warm places add jammy fruit aromas too, without making the wine sweet. None of these smells is sugar, which has no smell of its own: you can only taste it.

This is retronasal smell, aromas rising from the back of your mouth into your nose, and it explains the trap. Because fruit aromas reach your nose from inside your mouth, they feel like part of the taste, so a ripe, fruity wine can seem sweet when it is not. Sugar itself has no smell. Of the five basic tastes your tongue senses, sweet is the only one that tells you about sugar, which is why the nose-pinch test works.

Tasters call the meeting of sugar and acidity balance. A sweet wine with too little acidity can feel heavy and sticky; with plenty, the same sugar tastes lively and fresh. That is why a sweet wine with high acidity can seem barely sweet, and why alcohol, which tastes slightly sweet, can make a big, ripe dry red feel a touch rounder than it really is.

deeper.body: Sparkling wines use their own sweetness words. Brut Nature has under 3 grams of sugar per litre, with none added, and Brut, the most common Champagne, under 12. Confusingly, Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut, at 12 to 17, and Demi-Sec is clearly sweet, at 32 to 50. The sugar comes from the dosage, a little sweetened wine added just before the final cork goes in.

For ice wine, made in places like Germany and Canada, grapes freeze on the vine and are pressed while frozen, so only sweet, syrupy juice runs out. With so much sugar, the yeast stops before it can eat it all.
